dossier.public_summary: The 0.68-day dip is on the target and looks flat and planet-sized, but the star varies by the same amount and same period (≈10-25 thousand ppm) and the dip is much longer than expected for a planet. The measured depth nearly doubles between sectors. Together with a huge out-of-transit swing going in the same phase as the dip and a long duration, this matches a close stellar companion plus intense starspots much better than a small planet.

reasons.why: Light outside the 1.48-h dip swings as much as the dip itself and with huge chi2, classic for ellipsoidal/self-lensing of a close short-period binary with spots, not a small planet.

Duration 57% too long for a central transit around a 0.447 Rsun M-dwarf and formally requires star to be less dense even using Gaia radii; plus sectors instability indicates occultation on cooler/spotted star, not a planet.
reasons.value: observed_h 1.48, central_h 0.9407, ratio 1.574, fit_b 8.727e-13, fit_log_density_ratio -1.702, star_density_penalty 4348

reasons.why: Depth nearly doubles between sectors and is not a pipeline offset; with per-sector rotation amplitudes 10488-24952 ppm the variability itself can modulate the measured eclipse depth, not a stable planet.

Starspot period equals the 0.679-d dip period exactly, with tens of thousands ppm coherent modulation; real hot planets can share a period, but with phase-curve ratio ~1 and duration excess this is best explained as stellar rotation/activity driving the signal.

Flat-bottomed and no odd/even or secondary on its own would favour a small planet, but flat bottoms and no secondary do not rule out a small M-dwarf eclipsing binary at 1.49 h plus extreme spots; duration/phase-curve/stellar-modulation positives outweigh the benign transit morphology.
